items.title: Redis GETSET deleted our TTL and leaked a key forever
items.summary: Session state sits in Redis. Each session key has a 15 minute TTL, 900 seconds. A normal end deletes those keys immediately. The TTL only covers orphans: a crash, a dropped connection, any case where nothing calls cleanup. One of the keys is a counter, session:{id}:billableSecondsPending. It accumulates billable seconds while a session runs. A separate path collects that counter. Some of those keys outlived the session. They sat at 0, with no expiration, and Redis kept them. The increment is a Lua script. items.title: Modeling solar payback: the variables that matter and the ones that don't
items.summary: Modeling solar payback: the variables that matter and the ones that don't A 6 kW rooftop system at $3 a watt pays for itself in 8.8 years at average US electricity prices — but 5.0 years in California and 15.0 years where power is cheap. Same panels, same sun, triple the payback range. The panels are not the variable. Your electricity price is. Solar payback is usually sold as a single number — "pays for itself in seven years!" — as if it were a property of the panels. It is not. Payback is a ratio between what the system costs and what each kilowatt-hour it produces is worth to you, and both halves of that ratio vary wildly by house. The model itself is small enough to fit in one function. items.title: I built a zero-dependency library to estimate LLM API costs before sending a request

Nothing is broken; you simply had no idea what a request would cost until the invoice arrived. It is called llm-cost-estimator, it has zero dependencies, and it runs locally with no API key and no network calls. LLM APIs charge per million tokens, with different rates for input, cached input and output. Prices differ by model and change often. items.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
items.summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake. To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers. Things that were fun to get right: - Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes. - Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities. - Letting them in. Default log

items.title: React: estados de correo sin bloquear la interfaz
items.summary: En una interfaz de registro o verificación, el estado de correo no es un detalle del backend. Es una parte visible del producto: la persona pulsa un botón, espera una respuesta y necesita saber si puede continuar. Cuando ese estado aparece tarde, mueve el formulario o bloquea toda la pantalla, una operación correcta se siente rota. Este patrón me ha resultado util en flujos de React que prueban el envío de correo, incluso cuando se usa un fake email generator para crear datos de prueba. La meta no es hacer que cada cambio sea espectacular, sino que sea predecible, accesible y barato para el navegador. Un botón de “Enviar código” suele tener al menos cuatro estados: disponible, enviando, enviado y error. El problema aparece cuando la interfaz trata esos estados como una sola cosa. items.title: AlmaLinux Shows Advantages of ABI Compatibility After RHEL Restricted Source Code Access
items.summary: "AlmaLinux OS charted a new path in 2023 when Red Hat restricted source code access to Red Hat Enterprise Linux," remembers Linux Magazine. "Rather than pursue 1:1 compatibility with RHEL like other Enterprise Linux alternatives, the AlmaLinux OS Foundation chose application binary interface (ABI) compatibility, which guarantees that applications and kernel modules that work on RHEL will work on AlmaLinux OS." No longer constrained by the 1:1 promise, AlmaLinux can offer new features, or add back deprecated ones, while still remaining a stable, drop-in replacement for RHEL... The release of AlmaLinux OS 10.2 in May 2026 reveals just how far AlmaLinux has come.... When RHEL 10 increased the x86-64-v2 architecture baseline to x86-64-v3, many older server platforms (and some new ones) were left in the lurch. These older servers couldn't support the modern CPU feature sets in x86-64-v3, including AVX2 CPU instructions. AlmaLinux recognized that many community members employed older hardware that relied on x86-64-v2. items.title: A zero is not a measurement until you have run the positive control
items.summary: Everything below reads public files in dotnet/aspnetcore through the GitHub API. No clone, no build, no credentials beyond a logged-in gh. I ran each of these on 7 Nov 2026 against main. gh api "repos/dotnet/aspnetcore/contents/eng/test-configuration.json?ref=main" \ -H 'Accept: application/vnd.github.raw' Swap ?ref=main for ?ref=release/11.0 to check the shipping branch. Both end the same way: "failOnRules": [ ], "quarantineRules": [ ] } quarantineRules is empty. failOnRules is empty. Count the rules and all 14 are in retryOnRules, with localRerunCount: 3 above them. So every rule in this file weakens a guard by allowing reruns; none of them switches a test off. That distinction is the whole point — a retried test still fails the build when it fails deterministically. Note the Accept: application/vnd.github.raw header. Without it the contents API hands you base64 and you have to pipe through base64 -d, whose flag differs across platforms. The raw header avoids that entirely. gh api "search/code?q=QuarantinedTestAttribute+repo:dotnet/aspnetcore" --jq '.items[].path' That returns several paths; the definition is src/Testing/src/xunit/QuarantinedTestAttribute.cs. items.title: Rate limiting in Minimal APIs with .NET's built-in middleware
items.summary: This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: Rate limiting em Minimal APIs com o middleware nativo do .NET. Every API exposed to the internet will, sooner or later, get a client that decides to hit the same endpoint a thousand times per second. It might be a bug in a retry loop, a poorly written script or someone trying their luck. If you have no limit at all, the database, the CPU and your other users pay the bill. The good news is that since .NET 7, rate limiting ships with the framework. No extra package, no third-party library. In this post I build a small example with Minimal APIs, per-IP limits, a 429 response with Retry-After and integration tests. The middleware works with two concepts: the limiter (the algorithm: fixed window, sliding window, token bucket or concurrency) and the partition (who is being limited). Without a partition, the limit is global, and one abusive client takes the service down for everyone. Partitioning by IP gives each client its own bucket. You register a named policy and then apply it to the endpoints that need it. Endpoints like health checks usually stay out, otherwise the orchestrator may decide your application is down. builder.

items.title: How I prevent double bookings in Postgres (advisory locks + Supabase)
items.summary: I built a booking app for gyms with React, TanStack Start and Supabase. The part that looked easy and wasn't: two people booking the same slot at the same moment. This post explains the approach I ended up with, with a simplified version of the code. The problem A client opens the booking page, picks a service, a date and a time slot. Two clients can do this for the same trainer and the same slot within milliseconds of each other. If your app does this in two steps: SELECT to check the slot is free then both requests can pass step 1 before either one reaches step 2. Result: a double booking. Checking in the frontend or in your API code doesn't fix it, because the race happens between your two queries. Why not just a unique constraint? A unique constraint works if every booking uses exactly the same start time. It breaks down quickly: Services have different durations (30 min, 60 min), so bookings overlap without being equal. An exclusion constraint can handle simple overlaps, but group capacity ("up to 10 people") doesn't fit that model nicely. items.title: One codebase, two renderers: live previews in the browser, final renders in the cloud
items.summary: Our app, HypeFox, renders short videos from code: a model writes a scene file in JSON, and Remotion turns it into 1080×1920 frames on cloud containers. Last week we shipped an editor where people change a video and see the result right away. These are our notes from running the same video code in two places. The cloud renders with Remotion 4.0.536 on containers that sleep when there's no work (we wrote about that part here). The editor plays the video with Remotion's Player: same version, same style components. No style exists twice. Whatever the person changes is stored as overrides on top of the scene file: captions, texts, colors, transitions, elements. A save sends the overrides, and the cloud renders with the same code and the same overrides. The first thing we built was not a button. It was a check: two real videos, one with a generated voice and one cut from a person's footage, played by the Player in the browser and rendered by the same renderer we run in the cloud, then compared frame by frame. items.title: WeWeb or React: Which One Should You Start With?
items.summary: I get this question a lot, so I’ll answer it from what I actually did. On the recruitment ATS/CRM I worked on, the frontend was first built in WeWeb. Later we rebuilt the whole frontend in React 19 + TypeScript, and most of that work was done with Claude Code. So I’ve used both on the same product, with real users. My answer is simple: if you’ve never coded before, start with WeWeb. If you already have some notions of code, start with React. WeWeb is easy to pick up. You put elements on a page, connect them to your data, and add workflows that run when someone clicks a button or submits a form. What I like is that it teaches you how a frontend works while you build: What you pick up in WeWeb: how a page fetches data from an API where that data is kept while the page is open workflows: when this happens, do this, then that variables and conditions what to do when a request fails You do the same things in React later. In WeWeb you just do them visually first. It’s also a good option if you don’t want to vibe-code everything with AI. You build each part yourself, so you understand what you made. items.summary: Semi-retired professor Carolyn Marvin became a local celebrity facing down Philadelphia’s growing robot delivery army: ‘It’s my first amendment right to protest’ “One of you needs to be on the lookout for cops, while I block the robot, OK?” It is a crisp fall morning in Philadelphia. items.title: Put the Mongo-to-SQL toggle at the contract, not inside the shared package
items.summary: We are moving a feature from MongoDB to SQL. One team owns the Mongo side. A different team owns the SQL side. Both want the same common package and the same Function App, with as little code change as possible, and a simple toggle to switch between them. The obvious design is an if (useSql) somewhere. The question is where it lives. I think most people put it in the wrong place. The tempting spot is inside the shared package. One OrderService, one repository class, and a flag that picks the Mongo driver or the SQL client halfway down the call. It feels minimal. One file changes. It is also the version where two teams edit the same class. The Mongo team knows nothing about your SQL joins. The SQL team has never seen your aggregation pipeline. Within a month the flag has leaked into three methods, the tests need both databases running, and nobody can delete the Mongo branch because nobody is sure what it still covers. A toggle inside shared code means the shared code now has two owners and no owner. Put the toggle at the seam. items.title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
items.summary: Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago In early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn. As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process. items.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
items.summary: It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it. Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result. I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that. items.title: I Parsed the Same Format String Five Million Times
items.summary: I had an exporter writing CSV lines, one per row, millions of rows a night. Nothing clever in it: a string.Format call with a template and three values. It was slower than it should've been, so I put a profiler on it, and the call that lit up wasn't the file write or the decimal math. It was the formatting. Specifically, it was the part of string.Format that reads the template "{0},{1:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss},{2:F2}" and figures out where the holes are. That work was happening on every single call, and my template never changed. When you call string.Format(format, args), the runtime has to walk that format string, find the {0}, {1:...}, {2:...} placeholders, pull out the alignment and the format specifiers, and only then start stitching the output together. That parsing step is pure overhead if the template is a constant, which it almost always is. You wrote the template once in your source code. The runtime rediscovers its structure five million times. CompositeFormat is the fix, and it's about as simple as it gets. You parse the template once into a CompositeFormat object, then hand that object to string.Format instead of the raw string. items.title: A New JsonSerializerOptions Every Call Cost Me 120x
items.summary: A list endpoint on one of my services started showing up heavier in the traces than it had any right to be. It pulled a small object, serialized it, returned it. The payload was tiny — an order with three line items. But under load the thing allocated like it was streaming a video, and the CPU time didn't match the shape of the work. I went looking for the expensive query. There wasn't one. The expensive part was the return. Here's the line I'd written, more or less, inside the handler: var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, new JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase, DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull, Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter() }, }); Looks fine. It is not fine. That new JsonSerializerOptions { ... } sitting inside a method that runs on every request is the whole bug. I used to think JsonSerializerOptions was a settings bag — a few flags, a naming policy, done. It isn't. items.title: Vibrating Mattress Helps Clear Alzheimer's Protein From the Brain
items.summary: A vibrating mattress combined with two pills that release nitric oxide enhanced the brain's ability to clear an Alzheimer's-related protein. According to New Scientist, the experiment "caused the brain's blood vessels to swell and constrict more strongly, which enhanced the glymphatic system's clearance of [the protein]." From the report: [Kesa Kiviniemi at the University of Oulu in Finland] and his colleagues recruited 29 adults who hadn't been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or any other cognitive issues. The participants took a pill that dissolves when under the tongue, releasing nitric oxide. They then lay on a mattress that caused their bodies to gently vibrate for 40 minutes, taking another pill halfway through. Blood samples revealed that their levels of a type of protein called beta-amyloid 42 increased by 35 per cent, on average, after the intervention. This protein, which usually helps neurons signal and connect to each other, misfolds and form clumps in Alzheimer's disease. items.summary: Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient It was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up, many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable. items.title: Day 14: Extension Points on a Business Object and When to Override Them
items.summary: Behavior a definition can express needs no code written at all. The ones it cannot express are what needs taking over: what to check before this document is submitted, who to notify after it is saved, and under what circumstances a delete is not allowed. The way the framework offers to take over is inheriting from a business object and overriding a few of its steps. A subclass adds this form's own logic at the matching step as required, and the hard part is judging which step is the matching one, and whether that code belongs before or after base. A method name can only answer the order, with DoBeforeSave before the save and DoAfterSave after it. The rest has to be stated by the framework. items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found that TikTok violates the Digital Services Act because its For You recommendation algorithm can create a "rabbit hole effect," repeatedly exposing users to potentially harmful content involving topics such as sadness, isolation and body image. TikTok must change the feed's design or potentially face fines of up to 6% of its global annual revenue. The Verge reports: The findings come months after the EU Commission declared that TikTok's design is too "addictive." While TikTok has implemented controls to mitigate the algorithm's "rabbit hole effect," the Commission says its preliminary findings suggest that they're not effective. TikTok must now change the design of its For You feed, or else face fines of up to 6 percent of its global annual turnover. The platform is also facing pressure in the US, with lawmakers and a wave of lawsuits raising concerns about child safety. items.title: How I built a Wordle-style daily puzzle in SwiftUI (no backend)
items.summary: I recently shipped Gemdoku: Daily Block Puzzle, a 9×9 block puzzle for iPhone. The core feature is a Wordle-style Daily Challenge: every player in the world gets the same goal, the same move limit and the exact same sequence of pieces each day. It turned out to be a fun little engineering problem. Here's how it works under the hood, all in plain Swift and SwiftUI, with no backend. The obvious way to give everyone the same puzzle is to generate it on a server. I didn't want a backend. The game is fully offline, has no accounts and collects no data. items.title: Developer Pulls Roku's Popular Fish Tank Screensaver Following Fox Sale
items.summary: Roku is removing its popular Aquatic Life fish tank screensaver on December 1 and automatically switching affected users to Roku City. According to Cord Cutters News, the creator pulled the license after Roku's sale to FOX was announced. Ars Technica reports: The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium, from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing. Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen. He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku, a deal that closed today, Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn't be renewing Roku's license. "I can't be part of the Fox world," he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News' controversial style of news and entertainment. Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements, according to the user notice. items.title: OpenAI's New Cyber Model Found Ways to Attack Nearly 1,000 Linux Flaws

Axios reports: During testing, the system identified 1,724 security flaws and found ways to use 948 of them to gain administrator-level access to Linux systems for about $1.2 million in API credits. At least 10 of the techniques the model used were previously unknown, according to OpenAI. Human researchers reviewed the Linux findings before reporting vulnerabilities and proposed fixes to maintainers. The model also uncovered 81 previously unknown, high-severity flaws in Mozilla's Firefox browser. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.summary: Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development. The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Mining 14,351 Chess Puzzles with Stockfish 18 (and the Illegal-FEN Trap in chess.js)
items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.summary: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. I built Coincide as a native Mac app for the coding agents I already use. Here is a new 10-second motion preview: A Mac interface built with Swift and AppKit Coincide's main interface is built with AppKit, with SwiftUI where it fits, such as Settings. It brings native menus, Mac keyboard shortcuts, a native transcript and the agent/model picker into one window. The clip calls out the architecture: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. That describes Coincide's Mac interface. It isn't a benchmark or a claim that every workload is faster than another app. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Antigravity each run through their own command-line tool and existing login. Coincide does not sell or meter tokens. When you switch agents mid-thread, the next agent gets a recap of the turns it missed and works in the same directory. Each agent keeps its own native session. Switching back resumes that agent's session. The handoff deep dive covers the mechanism and its limits. The preview browses Codex, Claude Code and Cursor's picker catalogs. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece.
